chain.g: to escape a garment, get out of one's clothing

ety.text: From Middle English escapen, from Anglo-Norman and Old Northern French escaper ( = Old French eschaper, modern French échapper), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre (“to escape a garment, get out of one's clothing”, literally “to free oneself from one's cape”), from Latin ex- (“out”) + Late Latin cappa (“cape, cloak”). Cognate with escapade. Also doublet of scape.

senses.d: To get free; to free oneself.
ex: The prisoners escaped by jumping over a wall.
The factory was evacuated after toxic gases escaped from a pipe.

senses.d: To break out of confinement.
ex: The prisoners escaped their cell.

senses.d: To avoid (any unpleasant person or thing); to elude, get away from.
ex: He only got a fine and so escaped going to jail.
The children climbed out of the window to escape the fire.

senses.d: To avoid capture; to get away with something, avoid punishment.
ex: Luckily, I escaped with only a fine.

senses.d: To avoid responsibilities and stresses for a time.
ex: Work was stressful, and I needed to escape.

senses.d: To be forgotten by.
ex: I used to know the name of the capital of France, but it escapes me now.

senses.d: To elude the observation or notice of; to not be seen or remembered by.
ex: The name of the hotel escapes me at present.
The detective examined the crime scene, but one clue escaped his notice.

senses.d: To cause (a single character, or all such characters in a string) to be interpreted literally, instead of with any special meaning it would usually have in the same context, often by prefixing with another character.
ex: When using the "bash" shell, you can escape the ampersand character with a backslash.
Brion escaped the double quote character on Windows by adding a second double quote within the literal.

senses.d: To halt a program or command by pressing a key (such as the "Esc" key) or combination of keys.
To grow wild, instead of in a cultivated area.
ex: You have to be careful planting mint, or it will escape and take over your yard.

senses.d: The act of leaving a dangerous or unpleasant situation.
ex: The prisoners made their escape by digging a tunnel.

senses.d: Leakage or outflow, as of steam or a liquid, or an electric current through defective insulation.
Something that has escaped; an escapee.
ex: But what about the flocks of Waxbills? Are they escapes gone feral, or are they spreading from Africa?

senses.d: A holiday, viewed as time away from the vicissitudes of life.
escape key
The text character represented by 27 (decimal) or 1B (hexadecimal).
ex: You forgot to insert an escape in the datastream.

senses.d: A successful shot from a snooker position.
A defective product that is allowed to leave a manufacturing facility.
That which escapes attention or restraint; a mistake, oversight, or transgression.
ex: I should have been more accurate, corrected all those former escapes.

senses.d: A sally.
ex: thousand escapes of wit
